chunks: Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Qattan narrated to us. He said: al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Sukkari narrated to us from Muhammad ibn Zakariyya al-Jawhari. He said: Ibn Aisha and al-Hakam and al-Abbas narrated to us. They said: Mahdi ibn Maymun narrated to us from Muhammad ibn Abdullah ibn Abu Yaqub, from Ibn Abi Nu'm. He said:

I was present with Ibn Umar when a man came to him and asked him about the blood of the mosquito. So he said: Where are you from? He said: From the people of Iraq. He said: Look at this man! He asks me about the blood of the mosquito while they have killed the son of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family)! And I heard the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) say: Indeed they are my two sweet basils from this world — meaning al-Hasan and al-Husayn (peace be upon them).

key_terms.أهل العراق: The people of Iraq — reference to those in Kufa who invited Husayn and then betrayed him at Karbala
key_terms.البعوضة: The mosquito — symbolizing the triviality of the question compared to the enormity of the sin of killing the Prophet's grandson
key_terms.ريحانتي: My two sweet basils (rayhana) — a metaphor of tender love; in Arabic culture, basil is associated with being cherished and kept close

ai.seo_question: What did Ibn Umar say about the killing of Imam Husayn and the Prophet's love for al-Hasan and al-Husayn?
ai.summary: This narration records Ibn Umar's sharp rebuke of an Iraqi man who came asking about a trivial jurisprudential matter — the ritual impurity of mosquito blood — while the people of Iraq bore collective responsibility for the martyrdom of Imam Husayn (AS) at Karbala in 61 AH. Ibn Umar then cites the Prophet's declaration that al-Hasan and al-Husayn are his two 'sweet basils' (rayhana), a term of deep affection in Arabic culture denoting fragrant flowers that one holds close and cherishes.
